halbert_own_bugs.title: record_effect treats a non-zero-exit run_command as a successful effect
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: tools/executor.py:634-650 records on handler return; agents/state_machine.py:1210-1216 shows failure is encoded as 'Exit code N' inside the result string
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: Spoken tail says 'run_command: rm' for a command that failed (G4).
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: tools/executor.py:898-899 returns f'Exit code {returncode}\n{output}\n{errors}'.strip() as an ordinary handler return (and :933 the same for the pool path), so the executor takes the success branch and calls record_effect at :640-648 (run_command is in persona/guest_tools.py WRITE_PLANE_TOOLS, :50-56). agents/state_machine.py:1210-1216 confirms failure is encoded only as a string prefix the state machine must regex out of a 'success' result. On a voice turn the spoken tail (security/turn_digest.py:107-128 via state_machine.py:4200-4216) therefore reports 'run_command: rm' for a command that failed.

halbert_own_bugs.title: Spoken digest tail and its audit rollup bypass the registry and the guard
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: agents/state_machine.py:4192-4226 appends `tail` to spoken_segments and calls write_audit(summary=tail) after _echo_guard_egress ran at :4018; targets pass only ingestion.redaction.redact_text (turn_digest.py:88-99)
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: A write_file target path embedding an acked token is spoken aloud and written to the hash chain in clear (G5).
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: agents/state_machine.py:4192-4226 builds the tail from spoken_tail(...) after _echo_guard_egress already ran at :4018, appends it to spoken_segments, emits it as a speech_segment and calls write_audit(summary=tail) into the hash chain. The only cleaning applied to a target is security/turn_digest.py:85-95, which imports ingestion.redaction.redact_text (the pattern pass) — not get_global_registry().redact_text (the exact acked-value pass) and not the echo guard. A write_file to a path embedding an acked value is therefore spoken aloud and written to the audit chain in clear unless it happens to match a credential pattern. Same finding as G5's second half.

A05-echo-display-digest.summary: The echo guard's detection core (80-char window, whitespace normalization, every-offset scan, bounded chunk store, hash-only warning) is a faithful port of boot-echo-guard.ts, and the Hermes display seam (1000/16 tail-kept cap, one factory seam, no raw copy shipped) is ported and in one respect stronger. The port is not as solid as the origins in three places that matter in Halbert's own single-user setting: (1) the redact step behind the guard only replaces whole registered forms, so a partial or re-wrapped echo of an acked secret is flagged, logged as redacted, and delivered anyway -- OpenClaw suppresses the whole text; (2) the display seam exists only on live SSE events -- a timeline reload serves persisted tool blocks with raw args/results, which OpenClaw's history projection never does; (3) the seam runs the exact-value registry but not the forced pattern pass Hermes applies. The turn digest is stronger than OpenClaw's on content (redacted targets, raw args unrepresentable) but records only handler successes with no started/failed status, is unbounded, and its spoken tail bypasses both redaction layers. The streaming draft leak before the commit is Halbert's own and has no origin analogue. Durable-retry, multi-channel, provider-replay and envelope-strip invariants do not apply. Engine-side (Haloysius) implications: none for this unit.

halbert_own_bugs.title: Registration overwrites the per-job record, erasing last-run facts, and the catch-up run's completion lands on a different record — so every boot after the first re-serves an already-served slot
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED, and proved empirically with a throwaway snippet against SchedulerEngine (arch -arm64 venv python, temp persist_dir): add_job -> update_job_state('running') -> update_job_state('completed') writes completed_at; a fresh SchedulerEngine reads that completed_at back; a second add_job(Job(id='morning_report', ...)) then rewrites the on-disk record with completed_at = None. Code: engine.py:66-72 add_job unconditionally replaces self.jobs[job.id] and persists; executor.py:443-451 and 482-489 build Job() with created_at/started_at/completed_at unset. dashboard/app.py:254-264 reads prior_records BEFORE registration, which is correct for THAT boot only — the wipe lands on the record the NEXT boot will read. app.py:574-576 then sees _last_run_of == None and, for morning_report, app.py:578-585 only bounds it by the 12h max_age, so a second (and third) reboot inside the window each publish another morning report. The catch-up run's own completion cannot repair this: app.py:651 uses run_id = '<id>:catchup', so executor.py:696 writes morning_report:catchup.json, which nothing reads. tests/test_proactive_catchup_wiring.py:178-185 (test_registered_but_never_ran_still_catches_up) pins exactly the 'no timestamps' shape that every post-first boot now has, so this bug is currently PROTECTED BY A TEST — any fix must revise that test's premise. Design intent is on record: packet 03 line 274 specifies catch-up off 'last_run in the job JSON'. Highest-value single fix in the unit.

halbert_own_bugs.title: Task-level failures are recorded as 'ok' receipts and 'completed' state because the proactive tasks swallow exceptions and return {'status':'error'}
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED by reading both sides. scheduler/autonomous_tasks.py:505-507 (MorningReportTask.execute: except Exception -> return {'status':'error','error':str(e)}) and :559-561 (DetectorSweepTask.execute: same, 'non-fatal'). executor.py:660 takes any return value from _call_with_timeout and falls straight through to the success branch: :682-689 _log_outcome(success=True) with output=str(result) (the dict is stringified, never inspected), :692-693 anomaly_detector.record_job_outcome(True, job_id), :695 update_job_state(job_id,'completed'), :698 _finish_receipt(receipt_id,'ok'). A failed morning report is therefore indistinguishable from a delivered one in the record, the state and the receipt, and the anomaly detector is fed a success. Hermes's contrasting line is real (cron/scheduler.py:2992-2995: 'Empty final_response is a soft failure so last_status is not "ok"'). This and G8 are the same seam and should be dispatched together; the fix must decide whether tasks raise or return, because raising also re-enters the retry decorator (own-bug 3).

halbert_own_bugs.title: After a wall-clock timeout the task thread keeps running with live side effects while the receipt says 'error' and the retry decorator starts a second concurrent attempt of the same task
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED. executor.py:62-86 _call_with_timeout starts a daemon thread, joins with the deadline and raises TimeoutError while explicitly leaving the worker running ('the task thread is a daemon and is left to finish on its own'). TimeoutError is an OSError subclass and therefore an Exception, and utils/retry.py:26-33 defaults exceptions=(Exception,) while executor.py:572-580 passes only max_attempts/base_delay/max_delay/jitter/on_retry — so the TimeoutError is caught at utils/retry.py:81, slept on (utils/retry.py:92-99, capped at 60s with full jitter) and the whole wrapped body is re-entered, including mark_started at executor.py:651-654 and a fresh _call_with_timeout at :660, while the first task thread is still alive. executor.py:220 max_instances=1 constrains APScheduler submissions, not attempts inside one submission, and dashboard/app.py:1250 gives a 3-worker pool. Defaults make it concrete: timeout_s=600 and max_retries=3 (executor.py:406-408), so up to three overlapping DetectorRunner.run_all_sync() executions, each publishing findings. The 'error' receipt written at :748 is also false while attempt 1's side effects continue.

halbert_own_bugs.title: Restart-budget hold on clock rollback escalates to persistent safe-mode with a contradictory 'restart_budget_exhausted' line
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED on every element. restart_budget.py:45-52 returns BLOCK whenever now < max(restarts), before the window check. executor.py:349-371: `if decision is not RestartDecision.ALLOW` -> logger.error('restart_budget_exhausted job_id=%s restarts_in_window=%d max_per_hour=%d ...') where recent is computed as `now - t <= window_s`, which for a future stamp is a negative age and therefore counted — so the line can read restarts_in_window=1 max_per_hour=5 — and then guardrail_enforcer.enter_safe_mode(...). autonomy/guardrails.py:227-248 writes the flag and :270-280 re-arms safe mode from the file in a later process; executor.py:589-595 skips every job while it is set; dashboard/app.py:1252 sets enable_guardrails=True in production so the enforcer is not None. The relative-path observation is also correct: guardrails.py:244 uses Path('data/safe_mode_active.flag'), resolved against the process cwd rather than data_subdir, so where the daemon was launched from decides whether the hold is even findable. Precondition: restarts.json must hold at least one stamp, which only happens after an ALLOWed boot recovery (executor.py:373-374) — real but not everyday, hence medium not high.

halbert_own_bugs.title: Guardrail rejection leaves no receipt at all, so a 'rejected' run is invisible to the receipt-based liveness story
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED. In _wrap_task the safe-mode branch returns None at executor.py:589-595 (after update_job_state(job_id,'skipped', error='safe_mode_active')) and the GuardrailViolation branch returns None at executor.py:626-633 (after update_job_state(job_id,'rejected')). Both are before the receipt exists: mark_started is at executor.py:651-654. So receipts.json shows the last real run and then nothing, with no way to distinguish 'refused by policy' from 'the scheduler is dead'. run_receipts.py:43 carries blocked_config in the closed set for exactly this 'refused before spend' case and it has no producer (see G8). Low on its own, but a two-line addition inside whatever packet fixes G8/G11 — and without it the receipt file cannot support the liveness story it was lifted for.

halbert_own_bugs.title: _persist_restart_ledger keeps future-dated stamps and fsyncs the file but not its directory; _load_restart_ledger silently drops a malformed ledger
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED on all three sub-claims. executor.py:299-306: the prune keeps stamps where `now - t <= window`, trivially true for any t > now — so a future-dated stamp is retained forever and keeps max(restarts) > now, making own-bug 4's hold permanent rather than transient. executor.py:308-320: the write is tmp + flush + os.fsync(f.fileno()) + os.replace with NO directory fsync, unlike run_receipts.py:128-133 which does fsync the directory after the rename — so the rename itself is not durable across a power cut. executor.py:279-296: _load_restart_ledger catches (OSError, ValueError) and returns {} with no log, and silently returns {} for a non-dict top level, so a corrupt or hand-edited ledger hands a crash-looping job a fresh 5-restart budget at every boot with nothing in the log to say why. halbert_own_bugs.title: Monitor probe output with undecodable filenames raises inside evaluate(), so the gate never persists a baseline and the catch-up runs ungated on every boot
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED as a mechanism, with a platform caveat the founder should weigh. monitor_hash.py:171 is `digest = self.hash_fn(output_text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()` — strict — and I verified with a throwaway snippet that 'a\udcff'.encode('utf-8') raises UnicodeEncodeError while errors='replace' hashes fine. The probe really can produce surrogates: dashboard/app.py:436-445 builds its text from os.walk / os.listdir results, which Python returns surrogate-escaped for non-UTF-8 byte names. The raise happens at monitor_hash.py:171, i.e. BEFORE the persist at :175-179, and app.py:622-628 catches it and returns True ('running anyway') — so no baseline is ever stored and the same exception recurs at every boot, exactly as claimed. Hermes's contrast is real: cron/monitor.py:44-46 uses `output.encode("utf-8", errors="replace")`. CAVEAT: on Halbert's stated single macOS host this cannot fire (APFS/HFS+ enforce UTF-8 filenames, and the probe's only recursive target, /etc/systemd/system, does not exist on macOS — app.py:441 reports it 'absent'). It is live only on a Linux host, which is precisely the platform the probe was written for. One-word fix; dispatch as a chore, not a packet.

halbert_own_bugs.title: _is_fts_write_corruption_error contradicts its own docstring: a bare 'malformed' message is classified as FTS-scoped even when sqlite_errorcode says SQLITE_CORRUPT
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: Code confirmed at conversation_sqlite.py:866-891 (audit's 872-875/884-888 are right). Executed against the module: bare DatabaseError('database disk image is malformed') -> True, and True with sqlite_errorcode set to SQLITE_CORRUPT; the docstring at 872-875 says the opposite ('a bare malformed image is structural'). The origin's shape is hermes_state_fts.py:301-308 (not 312-321), where the message fallback is reached ONLY when errorcode is absent and additionally requires startswith('fts5:'). Nuance the fix must account for: this venv is Python 3.10.9, where sqlite3 exposes neither SQLITE_CORRUPT_VTAB nor exception.sqlite_errorcode (verified hasattr False for both), so today the errorcode branch is dead code and the message heuristic decides everything -- the `code is None` guard alone would not change behaviour here; the message test itself has to narrow.

halbert_own_bugs.title: add_open_loop and close_open_loop commit OUTSIDE the store lock on the shared connection, so they can commit another thread's half-built transaction
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: Mechanism confirmed: conversation_sqlite.py:3004-3011 (`with self._lock: INSERT` then `self._conn.commit()` after the block) and :3049-3057 (same for the UPDATE); every other writer in the file uses `with self._lock, self._conn:`, and the class docstring at 456-458 advertises 'Thread-safe (single connection + re-entrant lock)'. The second half is also right: if commit() raises, the INSERT sits in an open implicit transaction that the next `with self._conn:` on any thread publishes. BUT THE AUDIT'S ACTOR PAIR IS WRONG and should not be quoted to the founder: routes/conversations.py:73 builds a SEPARATE store instance with its own connection (so the peer-invoke path cannot join this transaction), and merge_thread (threads.py:582) and add_open_loop (threads.py:1085, via _sync_open_loops <- _refresh_receipt <- end_turn) are both reached through @_locked ThreadManager methods, so they are already serialised against each other. The real concurrent actors on the shared manager connection are the FastAPI threadpool routes that write through tm.store outside the manager lock: dashboard/routes/agent.py:2166 `tm.store.update_message(...)` and :2401 `tm.store.upsert_receipt(...)`. Either can enter its `with self._conn:` in the window after add_open_loop releases self._lock and before its commit() lands.

halbert_own_bugs.title: The open-path FTS block and _fts_recover catch only sqlite3.OperationalError, so a real SQLITE_CORRUPT (sqlite3.DatabaseError) from the index escapes and bricks the instance
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: Confirmed by reading and by running it. conversation_sqlite.py:688-690 (`except sqlite3.OperationalError` around the whole open-path FTS block) and :858-859 (the same in _fts_recover); _fts_recover is called unguarded from search (1156) and from inside write transactions (1289, 1379, ~1466, 2644). Empirical: with messages_fts_data corrupted on disk, the open-path backfill INSERT raises sqlite3.DatabaseError('vtable constructor failed: messages_fts') -- I checked the class explicitly, it is DatabaseError and not OperationalError, and sqlite_errorcode is absent on 3.10 -- it escapes to 757-767, `_conn = None`, and the store is dead on that open and every reopen (connected False, append_message None). Same outcome via receipts_fts_data. This is the mechanism behind G2 and it is the single highest-value fix in the unit.

halbert_own_bugs.title: The conversation store's default path ignores HALBERT_DATA_DIR while the state ledger honours it (CFG-1 applied to one store only)
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: conversation_sqlite.py:33 computes `_DEFAULT_DB` from Path.home() at import; :467 reads it at construction. continuity/state_store.py:168-181 `default_state_db_path()` resolves through utils.paths.data_dir() at call time with a docstring that names CFG-1 and the second-instance rationale, so the asymmetry is real and deliberate on one side only. Production default-path callers confirmed: routes/conversations.py:73, routes/guest.py:647, threads.py:1256 and 1265. tests/conftest.py:145-168 (autouse) sets HALBERT_DATA_DIR, which therefore protects the ledger and not the conversation DB. The same import-time home-relative default also exists in model/outcome_store.py:31 and somatic/store.py:27, so a fix should sweep all three.

halbert_own_bugs.title: forget_request has no error handling: any non-corruption SQLite error escapes as a raw exception, unlike every other store method, and on a runtime without FTS5 the unconditional `DELETE FROM messages_fts` aborts the forget
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: Confirmed at conversation_sqlite.py:2073-2103 (not 2129-2160): there is no try/except around `with self._lock, self._conn:`, the inner handler at 2090-2100 catches sqlite3.DatabaseError and re-raises anything `_is_fts_write_corruption_error` rejects, and the docstring promises a row count. That contradicts the class contract at 456-460, which names redact_message as the ONE method allowed to raise. 'no such module: fts5' is an OperationalError the predicate does not match (it only matches 'no such table: messages_fts' / 'no column named ... messages_fts'), so it re-raises and the DELETE FROM messages at 2101 never runs. Impact is low, though: the only caller, dashboard/routes/guest.py:647-655, catches Exception and reports the transcript forget as failed -- which in the fts5-missing case is honest, because nothing was deleted. Worth fixing for contract consistency, not as a correctness emergency.

halbert_own_bugs.title: StateStore.__init__ runs journal_mode=WAL / secure_delete / darwin pragmas unguarded, the exact failure shape conversation_sqlite documents as 'used to abort the migration'
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: Confirmed: continuity/state_store.py:305-322 runs connect, busy_timeout, `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`, secure_delete and the two darwin pragmas with no try/except, and the constructor then goes straight into `with self._write_txn():`. conversation_sqlite.py:536-548 documents precisely why that raises under contention ('a journal-mode change requires SQLite to grab an exclusive lock, and ... that lock request does NOT go through the busy handler') and tolerates it. The twelve in-process StateStore constructions listed in the audit are real (verified by grep: threads.py:904, threads.py:1227, recall.py:60, vault.py:168, provenance.py:215/299/376, executor.py:1067, watcher.py:360, write_config.py:117, editor.py:417, routes/state.py:44, guest.py:660), and threads.py:1229-1231 is the fail-soft branch that would silently disable consolidation for the process lifetime. The audit's own scoping is correct: on an already-WAL file the pragma is a no-op, so this is a first-boot-only race -- low severity, two lines to fix.

halbert_own_bugs.title: search_snippets returns [] while degraded instead of a LIKE fallback, so recall silently loses matching_messages exactly when the index is untrusted
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: Confirmed at conversation_sqlite.py:2570-2600 (not 2530-2557): `if not self._fts_recover(): return []`, and _fts_recover returns False for the whole degraded window (821-829). The consumer is threads.py:1181 (`self.store.search_snippets(t['thread_id'], query, limit=RECALL_SNIPPETS)`) inside the recall entry builder, so every recalled thread renders with no matching messages after any fail-open. The contrast the audit draws is accurate: search (1171-1192) does add a content LIKE fallback under exactly the same flag. The caller cannot distinguish 'no matches' from 'index detached'.

A08-store-hardening.refute_summary: 13 gaps checked against both sides; 10 stand, 3 refuted (G6 and G15 for architecture, G13 on the facts). Every origin claim held when read at the real lines, but the audit's line numbers are unreliable in both repos and must not be pasted into a packet unchecked: hermes_state_schema.py citations are shifted ~+150 (the FTS_STALE read is 836-843 not 1013-1022; _init_fts is 1020 not 1170; the file is only 1119 lines), hermes_state_fts.py's predicate is 301-308 not 312-321, preflight_db_writability is 532 not 428-470, _WRITE_PATIENCE_S is 349 not 23, and on the Halbert side upsert_receipt is 2339-2367 (not 2650), search_snippets 2570-2600 (not 2530), forget_request 2073-2103 (not 2129), append_message's user row is threads.py:407-415 (not 352-357). Substance re-verified at the true lines in every case. Four findings were confirmed by running code rather than reading it: a corrupt messages_fts or receipts_fts raises sqlite3.DatabaseError('vtable constructor failed'), NOT OperationalError, and bricks the store on that open and every reopen (G2 / own-bug 3 — the highest-value fix in the unit, and invisible to tests because _corrupt_fts_for_test only raises OperationalError); a NUL-filled file reproduces G8's log line verbatim; a v5 store with the unique index dropped and two open rows reproduces G14's permanent brick; and a chmod 0444 store reports connected=True while dropping every write silently, which makes G7 worse than written. G1's classifier bug reproduces, but the errorcode half is dead code on this venv (Python 3.10.9 has no sqlite_errorcode / SQLITE_CORRUPT_VTAB) and the origin's close-time-checkpoint suppression needs 3.12+, so I lowered it to medium. G5's preconditions are measured on this machine (SQLite 3.39.4, inside the origin's vulnerable range, with 5 conversation-store and 12 ledger connections per file in one process). G13 is refuted on evidence the audit got wrong: migrate_legacy_conversations runs on tm.store (dashboard/app.py:158), not a second connection, and both merge_thread and add_open_loop sit under ThreadManager's @_locked, so no in-process SQLite lock contention exists on the boot path it describes. All 7 own-bugs confirmed, with one scenario correction: own-bug 2's race needs dashboard/routes/agent.py:2166/:2401 as the second actor, not the peer-invoke route (separate instance) or merge_thread (same manager lock). gaps.proposed_test: monkeypatch INACTIVITY_SECONDS=0.5; run the swallowing loop above and, separately, `import threading; threading.Event().wait()`; assert `await asyncio.wait_for(_run(...), timeout=15)` returns a result dict whose error names the stop, and that `sys.stdout` is the original afterwards.

Log the leaked thread name. Document that an in-process thread cannot be killed (already in the docstring) — but the RUN must always return.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN (line numbers drift ~14 from the audit's citation, behaviour is there): hermes-agent/tools/code_kernel.py:659-673 _await_cell returns ('timeout', {}) unconditionally at the deadline and ('interrupted', {}) on the interrupt poll; :689-691 _cell_result calls _REGISTRY.discard(key, kernel) for both, with the comment 'No safe way to interrupt one cell in place: kill the kernel'; the kill path is code_execution_tool.py:736-756 (_kill_process_group, SIGTERM then SIGKILL after 5 s). HALBERT: execute_code.py:464-468 has no break on timed_out, so the first loop runs until done.is_set(); the grace loop at :470-474 is only reachable after done is already set. Verified empirically with arch -arm64 .venv/bin/python against the real module (INACTIVITY_SECONDS=0.5): both `while True: try: time.sleep(0.05) except BaseException: pass` and `threading.Event().wait()` were still inside run_script after 12 s and only ended because my own asyncio.wait_for cancelled them — nothing in Halbert wraps the handler in a wait_for (tools/executor.py has no wall clock; grep for wait_for hits only the shell-pool path at :886). The turn lock is real (agents/state_machine.py:342-376 turn_lock, :946-967 _acquire_turn_lock bounded by TURN_LOCK_TIMEOUT_S=600.0 at :232), so a wedged run does not merely lose one turn: every later message waits 600 s and is refused, until the process restarts. No compensating deadline anywhere in core or tests; no handoff doc defers it.

Nothing in script_rpc_host.py:93-132 checks whether the run is still live.
gaps.failure_scenario: A script starts `threading.Thread(target=poll, daemon=True).start()` where `poll` sleeps then calls `halbert_tools.frigate_get_latest_frame(...)` or `web_search(...)` in a loop, then prints a summary and exits. Verified empirically: with budget=1, 40 barrier-synchronised threads and sys.setswitchinterval(1e-9), a trial reached calls_dispatched=2 / budget_remaining=-1 (200 trials, first overshoot at trial 40; at the default switch interval 20 threads showed no overshoot). Real but narrow: it needs a script that fans out with threads, and the overshoot is bounded by the number of racing threads. One-line fix as proposed.

halbert_own_bugs.title: The deterministic AST gate misses obvious spellings of the very affordances it names
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/tools/execute_code.py:202-248: ImportFrom only checks whether the MODULE root is banned (:227-230), so `from os import system` passes; the Attribute check requires `node.value.id == 'os'` (:231-237), so `import os as o; o.system(...)` passes; only a literal `__import__('subprocess')` is caught (:238-247), so `importlib.import_module('subprocess')`, `getattr(os, 'sys'+'tem')`, `os.posix_spawn`, `os.execv`, `pty.spawn`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` all pass. Verified empirically by extracting scan_script_text from the file and running the ten shapes: only `import subprocess` and `os.system('ls')` were flagged. Tests :384-414 pin only the four caught shapes.
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: The gate's stated purpose (:206-214, 'refuses the named shell-out affordances ... so tool work stays on the tool pipeline where it is classified, gated and audited') is defeated by `from os import system; system('launchctl bootout ...')` — one line a model produces naturally when the direct form is refused with an error message that names exactly what was refused (:371-376). The docstring's 'a scan, not a sandbox' caveat covers dynamic strings, not these static shapes. Fix: track import aliases (`import os as X`, `from os import system as Y`), ban `importlib.import_module`/`__import__` with any banned or os-shell target, and extend _BANNED_OS_CALLS with exec*/spawn*/posix_spawn/fork and the `pty`/`asyncio.subprocess` modules — still deterministic, still a scan.
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED, reproduced independently against the real scan_script_text (execute_code.py:202-248). Flagged: `import subprocess` -> ['import subprocess'], `from subprocess import run` -> ['from subprocess import ...'], `os.system('ls')`, `os.popen('ls')`. NOT flagged (empty list): `from os import system; system('ls')`, `import os as o; o.system('ls')`, `importlib.import_module('subprocess').run([...])`, `getattr(os, 'sys'+'tem')('ls')`, `os.posix_spawn(...)`, `os.execv(...)`, `pty.spawn(...)`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(...)`. The code reason is exactly as stated: ImportFrom only tests the module root (:227-230), the Attribute branch requires a literal Name 'os' (:231-237), and only a constant-string `__import__` is caught (:238-247). Tests at tests/tools/test_execute_code.py:384-414 pin only the four caught shapes. Caveat for the founder, not a refutation: the module docstring (:25-30) already scopes this as 'a scan, not a sandbox' under F-1(a), so this is a gate that under-delivers on its own stated purpose (:206-214), not a claimed sandbox that leaks. Alias tracking + exec*/spawn*/pty/importlib coverage is still deterministic.

halbert_own_bugs.title: The monitor keeps injecting KeyboardInterrupt while the worker is unwinding, and can abort the worker's own finally before `done.set()`
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/tools/execute_code.py:464-468 injects on every 0.25 s tick once timed_out is true, and :470-474 keeps injecting during the grace period; the worker's finally (:453-457) runs `sys.stdout = capture.original; capture.close(); done.set()` — an async exception delivered between those statements aborts the finally and `done` is never set (then G1: the run never returns). PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc is delivered at the next bytecode boundary of the target thread regardless of what it is executing.
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: A slow script hits the inactivity limit, the first injection lands, the worker enters its finally, and the second injection (0.25 s later, or immediately if the first landed late) fires inside the finally: the capture is left half-closed and `done` is never set; the turn hangs. Fix: put `done.set()` first in the finally (or drive completion from `thread.is_alive()`/`thread.join(timeout=0.25)` instead of an Event), and inject at most once per 0.25 s only while `thread.is_alive()` with a bounded count.
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED as a mechanism, with the frequency caveat made explicit. The code is as cited: injection on every 0.25 s tick once timed_out (execute_code.py:464-468) and again throughout the grace loop (:470-474), while the worker's finally does three things before done.set() (:453-457). I reproduced the abort in isolation: a thread with a deliberately long finally, injected repeatedly, lost its finally in 20/20 trials (done never set, thread dead, KeyboardInterrupt raised out of the finally body); with a short finally and 0.5 ms injections it survived. In execute_code the finally is short but not free — capture.close() closes the spill file (a syscall that can block on I/O) — and the monitor keeps injecting for as long as done is unset, so the race retries until it either wins or loses. Losing it lands exactly in G1 (run never returns, turn lock wedged). Additional related hazard the audit did not name: the first loop injects after its sleep even if done was set during that sleep (:464-468), and CPython reuses thread idents, so a late PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc can in principle target a recycled tid. Both are fixed by the same change: set done first / drive completion from thread.is_alive(), and stop injecting once the thread is dead.

halbert_own_bugs.title: An in-flight tool call counts as inactivity, so one slow tool call (> 30 s) kills a productive run
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/tools/execute_code.py:396 sets activity at dispatch start and :409 at dispatch end; :405 `fut.result()` blocks with no timeout while the tool runs on the loop; the monitor (:466-468) sees > INACTIVITY_SECONDS of 'silence', sets timed_out and injects KeyboardInterrupt, which is queued until `fut.result()` returns (blocked in a C lock wait) and then fires — so the run is reported as stopped precisely when the tool call succeeds. The origin's per-call RPC timeout is 300 s (code_execution_rpc.py:91; stub code_execution_tool.py:281).
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: `halbert_tools.web_search(query=...)` on a slow link, or `frigate_get_events` over a large window, takes 45 s; the script is killed with 'script stopped: 30s with no tool call or output byte' although it was inside a tool call the whole time, and the tool's result (already computed and audited) is thrown away. Fix: count an in-flight dispatch as activity (an `in_flight` counter the monitor consults, or refresh activity from the loop side on a heartbeat while the future is pending). Test: fake tool that sleeps 2× INACTIVITY_SECONDS; assert success.
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED empirically. With INACTIVITY_SECONDS=1.0 and a registered recall_memory that awaits 3 s, the script `r = halbert_tools.recall_memory(query='3'); print('after', r)` returned after 3.0 s with {'error': 'script stopped: 1s with no tool call or output byte...', 'tool_calls_made': 1, 'budget_remaining': 24} — the run was killed precisely when the tool call succeeded, and its already-computed, already-audited result was thrown away. The mechanism is as cited: activity is stamped at dispatch start (execute_code.py:396) and in the finally (:409), but nothing refreshes it while fut.result() (:405) blocks, and the injected KeyboardInterrupt is queued in the C lock wait and fires the moment the future returns. Needs a real >30 s tool call at the default setting (web_search on a slow link, frigate over a large window), which is unremarkable. The audit's fix (an in-flight counter the monitor consults) is right.

halbert_own_bugs.title: Process-wide sys.stdout / sys.modules / sys.path mutation with no serialization — two overlapping runs corrupt each other and every other thread's print() is captured
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/tools/execute_code.py:269 `self.original = sys.stdout` captured per run; :447 `sys.stdout = capture` swapped globally from the worker thread; :436-439 `sys.modules['halbert_tools']` and `sys.path.insert(0, tmpdir)` global; :454-455 and :513-516 restore only `if sys.stdout is capture`. With two overlapping runs A then B: B's `original` is A's capture; when A finishes, `sys.stdout is captureA` is false so A does not restore; when B finishes it restores to captureA, which is closed — the process's stdout points at a dead capture from then on. Any coroutine or thread that prints during a run (e.g. index/chroma_index.py:357-364 flushes stdout) writes into the script's result. No lock anywhere in the module or the executor (grep: none).
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: Today the chat path is serialized by the turn lock (agents/state_machine.py:374, 960) and the MCP server is a separate stdio process (mcp/server.py:238, 1320), so this needs a second executor driver — a scheduled job, a peer/tool proxy or a future MCP-in-process route; it is latent, not live. Fix: a module-level `asyncio.Lock` (or a threading.Lock) making execute_code runs mutually exclusive with a clear 'another script is running' refusal, and per-thread stdout redirection is impossible in CPython, so document that stdout capture is process-wide.
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED in mechanism, with one correction and one strengthening. Code as cited: capture.original taken per run (:269), sys.stdout swapped globally from the worker (:447), sys.modules/sys.path global (:436-439), restores guarded by `if sys.stdout is capture` (:454-455, :513-514); grep for Lock()/Semaphore in tools/execute_code.py, tools/script_rpc_host.py and tools/executor.py returns nothing. CORRECTION: the cited index/chroma_index.py:350-368 only calls sys.stdout.flush(), it never prints, so that specific contamination example does not hold (there are ~215 print() sites elsewhere in the core, several in vision/ paths). STRENGTHENING: the 'needs a second executor driver, latent' framing understates it — a leaked worker thread from an earlier run (G1/G2) prints into a LATER run's capture with only one driver, which I hit by accident: after a wedged infinite-print run, the next run's stdout in my probe was full of the previous script's output. So the corruption is reachable today via G1/G2 and closes if those are fixed; the two-overlapping-runs half stays latent behind the turn lock (state_machine.py:342-376) and the out-of-process MCP server.

halbert_own_bugs.title: ScriptRpcHost.handle() can raise into the script on a non-ASCII token, contradicting its own contract
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/tools/script_rpc_host.py:88-91 `_token_ok` calls `secrets.compare_digest(token, self._token)` on str; Python raises `TypeError: comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported` (verified on 3.10.9). :93-95 promises 'the script never sees an exception from here'. The origin encodes both sides to bytes for exactly this reason (hermes-agent/tools/code_execution_rpc.py:33-38).
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: Only reachable by a script that reaches the host through `_call.__closure__` and calls `handle('é', ...)` — harmless in practice (the script's own exception), but a one-line fix: compare `.encode()` on both sides.
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED empirically: `ScriptRpcHost(...).handle('é', 't', {})` raises TypeError('comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported') from secrets.compare_digest at script_rpc_host.py:88-91, against the docstring promise at :93-95. Reachable only from script code that digs the host out of `_call.__closure__`, so the practical consequence is the script's own exception, not a policy hole — severity is 'contract tidiness', and the fix is the one line the origin already writes for exactly this reason (code_execution_rpc.py:33-38 encodes both sides, with the comment 'compare_digest raises TypeError on a non-ASCII str').

halbert_own_bugs.title: max_tool_calls=0 is treated as 'unset' and becomes the default 25
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/tools/execute_code.py:362 `budget = args.get('max_tool_calls') or DEFAULT_TOOL_CALL_BUDGET` — 0 is falsy; script_rpc_host.py:46 would otherwise honour 0 via max(0, ...).

A04-execute-code.summary: Halbert's execute_code faithfully ports the Hermes enforcement core (generated read-only stub module from an intersection, per-run secret token, fixed token→allow-list→budget→dispatch→log order with free refusals, capped head/tail stdout with a write-through spill, tmpdir/sys.path hygiene) and is stronger on policy: every stub call traverses ToolExecutor.execute with the guest floor and RoleGate cap, refusals carry the interactive audit shape, an empty intersection fails closed, and the stub module cannot be shadowed. The port is weaker exactly where Hermes relies on owning a child process. Three high gaps follow from the in-process thread model without compensating logic: (G1) the monitor loop has no deadline, so any script that swallows or never reaches the injected KeyboardInterrupt (an `except BaseException` retry wrapper, input(), Event().wait()) makes run_script never return and wedges the single turn lock until restart; (G2) the dispatch hook is never retired after a run settles, so a thread the script left behind — or the zombie from G1 or a cancelled task — keeps dispatching real tool calls under the old session and role (Hermes's CellAuthority.retire has no counterpart); (G3) output alone refreshes the inactivity clock and the spill is uncapped, so an infinite print loop never stops and writes to the host volume until it is full (Hermes caps the spill at 5 MB and has a 300 s wall clock). Medium gaps: stdout/traceback are not redacted before reaching the model and conversation store (redact_result exists but is only wired on the MCP surface — a founder-directive obligation, sharpened by the accepted unscrubbed in-process environment); `__name__` is not `__main__` so the standard main-guard idiom silently does nothing; partial stdout is discarded on error contrary to recover-don't-rerun; the schema never names the stub set so the model guesses at unavailable tools with no hint; stderr is not captured; a user stop does not interrupt a running script. Halbert-only bugs: the AST gate misses `from os import system`, `import os as o`, importlib/posix_spawn/exec*/pty shapes (verified empirically); repeated injection can abort the worker's own finally before done.set(); an in-flight tool call longer than 30 s is counted as inactivity and kills a productive run; process-wide stdout/sys.modules swapping is unserialized (latent until a second executor driver exists); compare_digest can raise on a non-ASCII token; max_tool_calls=0 becomes 25. Fixes are all small, deterministic and local to execute_code.py / script_rpc_host.py: bound the monitor loop, add ScriptRpcHost.retire() called from the run's finally, cap the spill and stop counting capped output as activity, route the result through redact_result, capture stderr, set __name__='__main__', return partial stdout on error, list the stub set in a per-turn schema, and poll a stop predicate. Engine-side (Haloysius) implications: none — the memory tools are reached only through the executor pipeline; note only that nested dispatch from the script thread has an empty contextvars context, which will matter for provenance turn_id once write-plane stubs are unlocked.

halbert_own_bugs.title: request_stop mirrors only half of cancel_session's paused rule: a turn paused on a confirmation while the lock is still held gets a flag nobody polls, and confirm_action then discards it
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: agents/state_machine.py:1667-1670 (request_stop takes the teardown path only when not _turn_in_flight()); 1633-1637 (cancel_session tears down when 'paused or not self._turn_in_flight()', and its docstring 1590-1598 names the sliver: 'the pause can be reached with the stream not yet drained — the generator suspended on its last event, still holding the lock'); 1502-1504 (confirm_action pops self.cancelled before resuming)
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: The turn breaks out of _drive on AWAITING_CONFIRMATION and is suspended on its last yield with the lock held; the user types '/stop' in that window: request_stop claims the generation, sets cancelled=True, returns 'stopped', the arrival's stream says cancelled — then the user's later confirm_action pops the flag and executes the staged action the user believed they had stopped.
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED, with the window narrower than the entry implies. The asymmetry is real: cancel_session tears down when 'paused or not self._turn_in_flight()' (state_machine.py:1633-1637), request_stop takes its teardown branch only on 'not self._turn_in_flight()' (:1666-1670) and otherwise claims the generation and sets the flag with no teardown. The window is exactly the sliver cancel_session's own docstring names (:1592-1598): process() holds turn_lock across every yield and releases it only in the outer finally (:832), and an async generator stays suspended AT its last yield until the consumer asks for the next item — so between the pause event being yielded and the SSE consumer draining it, _turn_in_flight() is True while the machine is in AWAITING_CONFIRMATION. In that window request_stop returns 'stopped', the arrival's stream says cancelled, and nothing polls: _end_turn and _settle_turn both return early while AWAITING_CONFIRMATION (:1000-1001), so the session stays in active_sessions and the flag sits there until confirm_action pops it at :1509. One correction to the framing: that pop is deliberate and documented for a different case ('A stop pressed while the confirmation dialog was open must not cancel the turn the user has just approved', :1507-1508). The defect is the missing teardown and the false 'stopped', not the pop itself. Narrow enough to rank low.

halbert_own_bugs.title: A voice arrival that is steered leaves its single-use relay receipt unspent
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: dashboard/routes/agent.py:1693-1710 (handle_midturn_arrival returns the arrival's stream before 1795-1800 where get_voice_relay_receipts().consume(request.relay_token) runs)
halbert_own_bugs.scenario: A spoken follow-up while busy is steered (the honest path) and the receipt bound to those words stays redeemable until expiry; the same transcript can later be re-POSTed as a whole voice turn carrying the relay's verified claim — a replay window the C2 receipt work closed for the turn path but not for the steer path.
halbert_own_bugs.verdict_reason: CONFIRMED. dashboard/routes/agent.py:1693-1710: when handle_midturn_arrival returns events (any steer or stop), the route returns the arrival's own StreamingResponse immediately — control never reaches the voice branch at :1795-1799 where get_voice_relay_receipts().consume(request.relay_token) runs. The receipt therefore stays in _pending, redeemable until TTL_S = 300 s (dashboard/voice_relay.py:94, consume at :135-149 pops single-use and rejects expired). So a spoken follow-up that steers leaves a live token bound to those words for up to five minutes, and the same transcript can be re-POSTed as a whole voice turn carrying the relay-derived claim/name/role. Impact is modest — the door is behind require_owner, the replay would mint the same identity for the same words, and the practical effect is the words being processed twice — but the asymmetry is exactly the one C2 closed on the turn path, and consuming the receipt on the steer path is the same one-line discipline.

A07-interrupt-algebra.summary: The pure core is faithfully ported (generation claim under one lock, single-shot, decline-not-double-fire; steer into the last tool result; observable verdict for every arrival; stale-flag hygiene; a stronger no-tool-result fallback and a more truthful stop outcome). Around it, three things weaken the port materially in Halbert's own setting. (1) The steer path runs before every admission gate the voice/claims work added: an unidentified voice speaker or a raw POST can inject text into the owner's running admin turn with no receipt, no role, no origin tag, and the injected marker is bare, so the model is told nothing about its authority — G1/G4 (high/medium). (2) The stop verb is weaker than Hermes's in three ways the packet did not intend: '/stop' during a tool is demoted to a steer (Hermes reserves 'yield, never kill' for guidance and hard-kills on /stop), a stop cannot abort an in-flight model request or a running subagent, and the dashboard's actual stop button bypasses the claim entirely via /api/agent/cancel — G2/G5/G7/G13. (3) Corrections that lose a race are confirmed then dropped (steer after stop, steer after commit, leftover at settle) where Hermes refuses them so they become the next turn — G3. The remaining gaps (queued-turn stop, liveness watchdog, ESTOP, auto-continue, yield, concatenating slot) are mechanisms the origin has around the algebra; all apply to a single-user host but two (auto-continue, ESTOP) are founder-policy questions first. REDIRECT stays dormant by a recorded verify-first finding; G5 is the primitive that would unblock it. Full JSON written to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-4TB-BAD-Halbert/b0e3f0dd-594e-4bec-b7ce-4859472b38f8/scratchpad/wf-oss/A07-interrupt-algebra.json.

A13-skills.refute_summary: All 13 gaps survive adversarial verification: every cited origin file:line was opened and implements the claimed behaviour, and every Halbert claim was re-checked against the whole core, the test tree and .handoff/DESIGN-SKILLS-SYSTEM-2026-09-07.md. Nothing is refuted. Four severities were lowered on verified grounds. G1 high->medium: the base classifier already covers the audit's own examples (safety.py:326-338 has '/boot/', :119/:134 block mkfs., injection_check blocks zpool destroy), so a malformed user file costs the entire skills plane silently but not the safety net -- the ValueError itself was reproduced live. G6 and G8 medium->low: both latent, since no bundled SKILL.md declares `requires` or `platform` and the skill_events consumers are SK-6/SK-7, which do not exist. G12 low with medium confidence: prompts/agent_prompts.py:45-67 already exposes a construction-time stable_prefix_key(), so only a consumer that text-splits on the marker is exposed, and none exists. G4's failure narrative was corrected (the catalog ladder does protect the prompt budget; what is unprotected is per-description length and the bundled-set discipline) and G5's urgency is tempered by the verified operator-owned-roots trust boundary (test_skills_trust.py:29-50) plus the HIGH-risk classification of writes under $HOME/.config/. G3 is the cheapest high-leverage item: OpenClaw emits explicit consultation guidance above <available_skills> in two places and Halbert emits none, so Track B works only if the model guesses the convention. All 10 halbert_own_bugs are CONFIRMED; six were reproduced live against the real modules (YAML alias x10-per-level expansion at 220-320 byte frontmatters; NaN budget_multiplier raising ValueError out of reallocate_budget; skill_for_path attributing every file under a root to a bare-layout skill; extends dropping an explicit child scalar and replacing rather than unioning requires; the /tank/data path-normalization bypass; the six over-60 bundled descriptions). One correction is material for dispatch: own-bug #5's '/boot' example does not actually bypass, because _classify_write (safety.py:723-732) uses a substring `in` test as well as startswith -- the exploitable class is skill-declared paths outside SENSITIVE_PATHS, symlink aliases, and the '/bootleg' prefix over-match. gaps.title: Non-JSON-native values skip the choke point and are stringified after it (json.dumps default=str)
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/logging/redact.ts:1167-1169 leaves non-plain objects untouched, but every surface that writes text redacts the serialized string: logger-redaction-behavior.test.ts:47-66 (file log line), node-worker-output.ts:40-44 (raw JSON text redacted before parse), proxy-capture/runtime.ts:285-297 (non-UTF-8 buffers omitted once any secret is registered)
gaps.halbert_evidence: security/result_redaction.py:120-129 returns anything that is not str/dict/list/tuple as-is; mcp/server.py:1281-1284 then json.dumps(result, default=str) and ships the text with no further pass. Probe: {'note': Obj()} with __str__ 'password=hunter2-objsecret' and {'blob': b'password=hunter2-objsecret'} both serialize the secret raw after redact_result.
gaps.failure_scenario: A tool handler (e.g. _tool_get_discoveries at mcp/server.py:179 returns d as-is when it lacks to_dict; a future handler returns a Path, an Enum, a dataclass, a datetime-keyed object, or bytes read from a config file) places a value whose str() contains a credential into its result. mcp_response passes it untouched, json.dumps(default=str) renders it, and the cloud-forwarding MCP client receives the plaintext secret. The dispatch-level choke point the Tier 2 guarantee rests on is bypassed by type, not by a forgetful handler.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_tier2_guarantee.py: register a handler returning {'note': _Obj()} (custom __str__ containing 'password=hunter2-obj'), {'blob': b'token=hunter2-bytes'}, {'p': pathlib.PurePosixPath('/x/password=hunter2-path')}; assert none of the three sentinels appear in resp['result']['content'][0]['text'] and '<secret>' does.
gaps.proposed_fix: Two layers: (1) in result_redaction._redact_value, coerce before redacting — bytes -> decode('utf-8','replace') then the string branch; any other non-native scalar -> str(value) then the string branch (mirror the default=str the serializer will apply); (2) in mcp/server.py:1283, run redact_text(prose=True) + get_global_registry().redact_text over the serialized JSON text as a second, text-level pass (the origin's surface-write pattern). Keep the parity test (test_result_redaction.py) and add the coerced shapes to CASES.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified. openclaw/src/logging/redact.ts:1144-1146 isPlainRedactableObject + :1178-1180 'if (!isPlainRedactableObject(value)) return value' (the audit cited 1167-1169, which is the [Circular] branch — ~11 lines of drift, mechanism present). The surface-write pattern is real: node-host/node-worker-output.ts:61 redacts the RAW JSON TEXT before JSON.parse (redactLaunchText at :40-44 = scrub -> registry -> patterns), and proxy-capture/runtime.ts:286-300 decodes UTF-8 buffers to text and redacts, or omits non-UTF-8 buffers entirely once any secret is registered. HALBERT: verified by probe. security/result_redaction.py:129 returns unknown types as-is; mcp/server.py:1281 mcp_response(...) then :1283 json.dumps(result, default=str) with no text-level pass. Probe (arch -arm64 .venv/bin/python): {'note': Obj(__str__='password=hunter2-objsecret')} -> '"note": "password=hunter2-objsecret"'; bytes -> "b'password=hunter2-bytes'"; PurePosixPath -> '/x/password=hunter2-path'. STRONGER THAN THE AUDIT SAID: types.MappingProxyType is not a dict, so it bypasses the STRUCTURAL rules too — redact_result({'env': MappingProxyType({'password':'hunter2'})}) returns the mapping untouched and json.dumps renders "{'password': 'hunter2'}". MCPServerConfig.env is exactly a MappingProxyType (mcp/config.py:234), so this is not hypothetical typing. No second text pass exists anywhere: grep of mcp_response( call sites and federation/fleet_proxy.py shows only structural redaction; no test in tests/test_result_redaction.py, test_mcp_response_boundary.py or test_tier2_guarantee.py exercises bytes/Path/Enum/mappingproxy. Reachability today: mcp/server.py:179-180 returns discovery objects as-is when they lack to_dict, and Discovery.to_dict (discovery/schema.py:252) passes an arbitrary scanner-supplied 'data' dict through. The existence of default=str at :1283 is itself evidence non-native values reach the serializer. Severity held at high: this is a type-shaped bypass of the one choke point the Tier 2 guarantee rests on, it is silent, and the fix is small.

gaps.title: Registry pass runs after the pattern pass, so a pattern rewrite inside a registered value defeats exact matching and leaks the remainder
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/logging/redact.ts:880 (redactRegisteredSecretValues first, then redactText), :951, :979, :1021, :1227 — every text path is exact-first
gaps.halbert_evidence: security/result_redaction.py:120-122 (redact_text first, registry second); PACKET-05 Task A3 step 1 asserts the reverse order is safe. Probe: acked 'tok-203.0.113.5-end' -> 'the value tok-<ip>-end is set'; 'pw-eyJabc.def.ghi-zz' -> 'pw-<jwt>-zz'; 'abc.user@example.com.xyz' happens to be fully swallowed only because EMAIL_RE consumed the whole token.
gaps.failure_scenario: The user acknowledges egress of a Tier 2 value that embeds a public IP, a MAC, a JWT-shaped segment, an email or an @-credential fragment (common in connection strings and composite API keys). The pattern pass replaces the inner shape with '<ip>'/'<jwt>', the registry no longer finds the exact form, and the surrounding prefix/suffix of the secret (often the discriminating part) reaches the MCP client, the display seam and the echo-guard seam in every later response.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_result_redaction.py: register 'tok-203.0.113.5-end' and 'pw-eyJabc.def.ghi-zz' in a fresh global registry; assert redact_result({'note': f'the value {s} is set'})['note'] == 'the value <secret> is set' for both (no 'tok-' or '-zz' residue).
gaps.proposed_fix: Swap the order in _redact_value: registry first (exact forms are unaffected by later pattern passes, the reverse is not true), then redact_text. Also apply the same order in display_transport.verbose_text if a pattern pass is ever added there, and in the server catch-all (G5). Update the docstrings that claim the reverse order is safe.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified exactly, line for line. openclaw/src/logging/redact.ts:880 (redactSensitiveText: registry first, patterns after), :951, :979, :1021, :1227 — every one of those four line numbers is a redactRegisteredSecretValues call feeding its output into the pattern pass. Exact-first is universal in the origin. HALBERT: verified. security/result_redaction.py:120-122 does redact_text() then get_global_registry().redact_text(). PACKET-05 Task A3 step 1 (.handoff/OPENCLAW-LIFT-PACKET-05-SECURITY-HARDENING-2026-09-07.md:193) states the reverse order 'is safe' — a stated rationale, not a recorded trade-off, and it is wrong. Probe: with 'tok-203.0.113.5-end' registered, redact_result({'note': 'the value tok-203.0.113.5-end is set'}) -> 'the value tok-<ip>-end is set' (prefix 'tok-' and suffix '-end' survive). Second probe corrected: 'pw-eyJabc.def.ghi-zz' -> 'pw-<jwt>' — JWT_RE eats the '-zz' too, so the residue is 'pw-' not the audit's 'pw-<jwt>-zz'. Residue is a fragment, not the whole secret, hence medium not high; but the reorder is a two-line change and strictly dominates (exact forms are unaffected by a later pattern pass, the converse is not true), and it also removes the G11 placeholder collision on pattern-produced markers.

gaps.title: Raw secret form is not registered newest; FIFO eviction can drop the live value while keeping only encoded variants
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/logging/secret-redaction-registry.ts:31-44 (encoded forms first, raw last, with the comment explaining eviction safety); redact.test.ts:109-122
gaps.halbert_evidence: ingestion/redaction_registry.py:43 (sorted(forms)) and :54-60 (inserted in that order; eviction after each insert). Probe: value 'a"b c d' with max_entries=2 leaves entries ['a%22b%20c%20d', 'a\\"b c d'] and the raw form absent.
gaps.failure_scenario: Over a long-lived session with many acked values (or a secret whose raw form sorts before its encoded forms) the 512-form bound is reached; the next registration evicts the oldest entries, which for such values is the raw form. The registry then redacts only the URL/JSON-escaped renderings while the plaintext value — the one that actually appears in prose tool results — passes.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_redaction_registry.py: reg = SecretVariantRegistry(max_entries=2); reg.register('a"b c d'); assert 'a"b c d' in reg. Plus a churn test: register 600 distinct values whose raw form sorts first; assert the last value's raw form is present.
gaps.proposed_fix: In register(): iterate the encoded variants (excluding the raw) first, then insert/move the raw value last; do not sort. Optionally evict per value rather than per form so a value's forms live or die together.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified. openclaw/src/logging/secret-redaction-registry.ts:31-44 registers encodeURIComponent form, then JSON-escaped form, then the raw value last, with the comment at :42-44 'Keep the raw value newest so bounded-registry eviction cannot drop the active credential while retaining only a transformed representation'. redact.test.ts:97-122 pins eviction and recency (the audit's :109-122 is the recency test, not the raw-last invariant itself; the invariant lives in the source comment). HALBERT: mechanism confirmed — ingestion/redaction_registry.py:43 sorted(forms) and :54-60 insert-then-evict. BUT THE FAILURE SCENARIO AS WRITTEN IS WRONG AT THE REAL BOUND. Probe with the production max_entries=512: after registering 600 distinct values whose raw form sorts first, the NEWEST value's raw form is present; only the value sitting at the eviction frontier (index 429 in the probe) shows the raw-gone/encoded-kept split, and that value is one or two registrations from full eviction anyway. The audit's own proposed churn test ('register 600 ... assert the last value's raw form is present') PASSES today, unfixed. The audit's dramatic result needed max_entries=2, which no call site uses (get_global_registry() takes the default; grep shows no other SecretVariantRegistry construction in halbert_core). Real, cheap to fix for fidelity, but near-inconsequential — severity dropped medium -> low.

gaps.title: MCP client credentials (bearer tokens, server env values, URL-borne secrets) are never registered in the variant registry
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/agents/mcp-connection-resolver.ts:157-183 registers every resolved header value, the bare token, the full URL, each query value and the URL password before the connection can reach a transport; mcp-connection-resolver.test.ts:454-483 pins it; secrets/sentinel.ts:54, :62, :103 register at every resolution
gaps.halbert_evidence: grep shows the only registration site is config/queries.py:359. mcp/config.py:183-196 resolve_token returns the literal or env-var token without registering it; mcp/config.py:234 passes per-server env through unregistered; mcp/client.py:193-200 (_scrub) and :586-589 only scrub the token from that module's own exception strings.
gaps.failure_scenario: An HTTP MCP server configured with auth.token_env echoes its request headers in a tool result (debug/echo tools do), or a stdio server started with env: {API_KEY: ...} prints the key in an error line. The bridge result flows to the local model, is emitted through StreamEvent.tool_complete (display_transport.py:82-84 registry-only), persisted to the conversation store, and — via the compute endpoint or the fleet proxy — could be re-served through mcp_response, where neither a bare token nor an env value matches any pattern. The registry, which exists for exactly this class, knows nothing about it.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_mcp_client.py (or a new test): configure an MCPServerConfig with auth.token='tok-registry-sentinel-12345' and env={'X': 'env-registry-sentinel-67890'}; construct the client / resolve the token; assert both values are in get_global_registry(); then assert verbose_text('echo tok-registry-sentinel-12345') == 'echo <secret>'.
gaps.proposed_fix: At MCPAuthConfig.resolve_token (mcp/config.py:183) and at server-config load for env values, call get_global_registry().register(value) (plus the bare token if the header is scheme-prefixed, and the URL password/query values when a URL carries them, mirroring mcp-connection-resolver.ts). Replace client.py's ad-hoc _scrub list with the registry pass so there is one learned layer.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified precisely. openclaw/src/agents/mcp-connection-resolver.ts:160-185 registerResolvedConnectionSecrets registers every header value, the bare scheme-stripped token, the full resolved URL, every query value and the URL password, with the doc comment at :155-159 giving the reason; mcp-connection-resolver.test.ts:454-482 pins all four assertions. HALBERT: verified — grep of the whole core for get_global_registry shows the ONLY register() call site is config/queries.py:359 (inside get_config_value's ack path). mcp/config.py:183-210 resolve_token returns the literal/env token with no registration; MCPServerConfig.env (mcp/config.py:234) is never registered; mcp/client.py:193-200 _scrub only string-replaces the token in that module's own exception text (used at :589). MCP-client tool results reach the model with no redaction at all (mcp/bridge.py:161-180 format_tool_result -> json.dumps, grep 'redact' in bridge.py finds only docstrings). SEVERITY DOWN medium -> low for two reasons. (1) The origin's motivation is its debug-proxy capture and log redaction, neither of which Halbert has. (2) A structural fact the audit missed: config.queries.get_config_value is imported ONLY by mcp/server.py, and dashboard/routes/guest.py:5-6 records that mcp/server.py is a STANDALONE stdio/HTTP process while the dashboard process owns the agent — so the process-global registry in the agent process is permanently EMPTY today. Registering client credentials would be the first thing to populate it, which is a genuine (if modest) strengthening rather than a leak fix. Partial coverage already exists for the token in client error strings.

gaps.title: MCP dispatcher catch-all redacts the error text with patterns only; the registry pass is skipped
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/node-host/node-worker-output.ts:40-44 and :46-55 (diagnostic text: scrub -> registry -> patterns); redact.ts:876-897 (the shared text path always begins with redactRegisteredSecretValues)
gaps.halbert_evidence: mcp/server.py:1300-1305 uses ingestion.redaction.redact_text alone; tests/test_tier2_guarantee.py:107-124 only pins a pattern-shaped sentinel ('sk-live-...'), not a registered bare value
gaps.failure_scenario: After the user acks a Tier 2 value (say a short opaque password with no vendor prefix), a handler crashes with ValueError(f'cannot parse credential: {value}'). No pattern matches a bare value; the registry would, but is not consulted; the JSON-RPC error message carries the acked plaintext to the MCP client — the one path the choke point does not cover.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_tier2_guarantee.py: register 'opaque-acked-value-9' in a fresh global registry; install a handler that raises ValueError('bad: opaque-acked-value-9'); assert the sentinel is absent from json.dumps(resp) and '<secret>' is present.
gaps.proposed_fix: Introduce security/result_redaction.redact_error_text(msg) = get_global_registry().redact_text(redact_text(msg, prose=True)) (registry first per G2) and use it in server.py:1305, mcp/client.py:_redact, and mcp/config.py:_redact, so every error-string surface shares one implementation.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified. openclaw/src/node-host/node-worker-output.ts:40-44 redactLaunchText = scrubCredential -> redactRegisteredSecretValues -> redactToolPayloadText, used by sanitizeNodeWorkerDiagnostic at :46-55 and parseNodeWorkerOutputJson at :57-73; redact.ts:876-899 confirms the shared text path always begins with the registry. HALBERT: verified. mcp/server.py:1305 returns self._error(req_id, -32603, redact_text(f'Internal error: {e}')) — patterns only, registry skipped; tests/test_tier2_guarantee.py:107-124 pins only a pattern-shaped sentinel 'sk-live-abcdef1234567890abcdef'. This is the LIVE one of the medium gaps: queries.py:359 register() runs in the same process as the dispatcher, so the registry there is genuinely populated. CORRECTION to the audit's proposed sentinel: redact_text('cannot parse credential: opaque-acked-value-9', prose=True) already yields 'cannot parse <secret>' because 'credential' is a secret key with a ':' separator — the test must avoid a key-shaped context. Verified bare case: redact_text('Internal error: bad: hunter2', prose=True) returns it unchanged, so an acked value in an exception message with no key context does cross. The same skip applies to mcp/client.py:183-190 _redact and mcp/config.py:136-145 _redact, both redact_text-only.

gaps.title: Minimum registrable length is 4, not 6; four- and five-character acked values blanket-redact ordinary prose
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/logging/secret-redaction-registry.ts:4, :28-30; redact.test.ts:72-76
gaps.halbert_evidence: ingestion/redaction_registry.py:29, :52-53; PACKET-05 Task A1 step 3 sketch sets 4 with no rationale. Probe: register('pass') -> 'bypass the password field' becomes 'by<secret> the <secret>word field'.
gaps.failure_scenario: The user acks a short Tier 2 value such as 'root', 'pass', 'true', '1234' or 'admin'. From then on every MCP result, every tool_start/tool_complete display event and every echo-guard-flagged reply has that substring replaced process-wide — 'bypass', 'passphrase', 'enabled=true', file paths containing 'root' — corrupting config text and tool output (Hermes issue #35519 class: masked text written back). Conversely a 4-char value gives no real protection, since it collides with prose anyway.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_redaction_registry.py: reg.register('pass'); assert len(reg) == 0 and reg.redact_text('bypass') == 'bypass'; keep the existing 'ab' case.
gaps.proposed_fix: Raise MIN_SECRET_VARIANT_LEN to 6 to match the origin; if short acked values must still be protected, register them only with word-boundary matching (a compiled alternation with \b) rather than substring replacement.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified. openclaw/src/logging/secret-redaction-registry.ts:4 MIN_SECRET_VALUE_LENGTH = 6, enforced at :28-30; redact.test.ts:72-75 'ignores values shorter than six characters' pins it with 'abcde'. HALBERT: verified. ingestion/redaction_registry.py:29 MIN_SECRET_VARIANT_LEN = 4, enforced at :43 and :52-53; the packet sketch (.handoff/OPENCLAW-LIFT-PACKET-05-SECURITY-HARDENING-2026-09-07.md:124) sets 4 with no rationale given — an imprecise port, not a recorded decision. Probe: reg.register('pass') then reg.redact_text('bypass the password field') -> 'by<secret> the <secret>word field'. Real consequence: once a 4- or 5-char Tier 2 value is acked, every later MCP config result out of that process has that substring blanked, which corrupts config text the remote client reads and acts on. Held at medium. Note the trade-off the fix carries: raising the floor to 6 removes protection for genuinely short acked secrets, so the word-boundary alternative in the audit's proposed_fix is the better shape.

gaps.title: Only urllib.parse.quote's encoding is registered; encodeURIComponent-style ('%2F') and quote_plus ('+' for space) surface forms evade the registry
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/logging/secret-redaction-registry.ts:31-35 (encodeURIComponent); redact.test.ts:78-85 pins 'path/token with+reserved%chars'
gaps.halbert_evidence: ingestion/redaction_registry.py:42 uses urllib.parse.quote(value) (safe='/'). Probe: 'p@ss w/rd' registers 'p%40ss%20w/rd'; requests/urlencode emit 'p%40ss+w%2Frd', and JS clients emit 'p%40ss%20w%2Frd' — neither is registered.
gaps.failure_scenario: An acked secret containing '/' or a space (base64 values contain '/') is placed by the agent into a URL query or a form body via requests; the tool result or an HTTP error echoes the encoded URL. The registered form differs by one escape, the exact match fails, and the encoded secret passes the MCP boundary and the display seam — the exact leak class the packet cites as the reason for the lift.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_redaction_registry.py: reg.register('p@ss w/rd'); for enc in (quote_plus(v), quote(v, safe="-_.!~*'()")): assert reg.redact_text(f'see {enc} here') == 'see <secret> here'.
gaps.proposed_fix: In _variants_of, register urllib.parse.quote(value, safe="-_.!~*'()") (encodeURIComponent-equivalent) and urllib.parse.quote_plus(value) in addition to quote(value).

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified. secret-redaction-registry.ts:31-35 registers encodeURIComponent(value); redact.test.ts:78-85 pins exactly the awkward case — secret = 'path/token with+reserved%chars' — asserting the encoded form is masked. HALBERT: verified by probe. ingestion/redaction_registry.py:42 uses urllib.parse.quote(value), whose default safe='/' leaves '/' unescaped. For v = 'p@ss w/rd' the registry holds only ['p%40ss%20w/rd', 'p@ss w/rd']; redact_text on quote_plus(v) = 'p%40ss+w%2Frd' and on quote(v, safe="-_.!~*'()") = 'p%40ss%20w%2Frd' both return the text UNTOUCHED. The origin's own test case is precisely the case Halbert misses, so this is a clean fidelity miss with a one-line fix. Severity low because it needs an acked secret containing '/' or a space to be re-encoded by requests/urlencode and echoed back.

gaps.title: Redaction seams fail open on exception, and the unsynchronized global registry makes that path reachable
gaps.origin_evidence: hermes-agent/tui_gateway/tool_progress.py:38-44 (exception -> '' ); tests/test_tui_gateway_server.py:1530-1541; hermes-agent/agent/redact.py:801, :862-865 (registry lock)

gaps.failure_scenario: An acked get_config_value on the MCP HTTP thread calls register() while the dashboard thread is inside _sorted_forms()'s sorted(self._variants) (or a popitem happens mid-iteration): CPython raises RuntimeError('OrderedDict mutated during iteration'). At the reply seam that exception is swallowed and the unredacted reply is delivered; at the display seam it propagates and breaks the tool_complete event.
gaps.proposed_test: (1) tests/test_redaction_registry.py: two threads, one registering 5,000 distinct values, one calling redact_text in a loop; assert no exception. (2) tests/test_display_transport.py: monkeypatch get_global_registry().redact_text to raise; assert verbose_text('secret text') == '' (fail closed) and that StreamEvent.tool_complete still constructs.
gaps.proposed_fix: Add a threading.Lock to SecretVariantRegistry guarding register() and the cache rebuild (snapshot the tuple under the lock, scan outside it). Make verbose_text and the two seams fail closed: on exception return '' (display) or the placeholder-only text (reply), and log at warning with a hash, never the text.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: both cites verified, with one mischaracterisation. hermes tui_gateway/tool_progress.py:38-44 _redact_tui_verbose_text returns '' on any exception (fail closed), pinned by tests/test_tui_gateway_server.py:1530-1541. hermes agent/redact.py:802 _registry_lock = threading.Lock(), taken at :863-865 and :872-874 — but that lock guards the PLUGIN PATTERN registry, not a secret-value registry; Hermes has no locked secret-value registry, so 'Hermes guards its registry with a lock' is only loosely true and its motivation (plugin load/unload) is a multi-extension context Halbert does not have. HALBERT — THE STATED FAILURE SCENARIO CANNOT OCCUR AS WRITTEN, on two independent counts. (1) Wrong processes: dashboard/routes/guest.py:5-9 records that mcp/server.py is a standalone stdio/HTTP process and only the dashboard process owns the agent; nothing outside mcp/server.py imports MCPServer, and config.queries.get_config_value is imported only by mcp/server.py. So 'an acked get_config_value on the MCP HTTP thread while the dashboard thread is inside _sorted_forms()' spans two processes with two separate globals — and the agent-process registry is in fact permanently empty today. (2) Wrong mechanism: RuntimeError('OrderedDict mutated during iteration') is not reachable — sorted(od, key=len, reverse=True) is entirely C-level under the GIL. A 5-thread / 90,000-iteration probe (2 writers registering, 3 readers redacting, max_entries=1e6) produced zero exceptions and zero unredacted passes. WHAT IS REAL: ingestion/redaction_registry.py:45-72 has no lock and mcp/server.py:1860-1861 is a ThreadingHTTPServer, so two concurrent get_config_value requests in that one process can race; the actual failure mode is not RuntimeError but _sorted_forms() at :70-72 returning None when register()'s 'self._sorted_cache = None' (:61) lands between the assignment and the return, after which redact_text's 'if not forms: return text' (:87-88) fails OPEN. A threading.Lock is worth the two lines. The fail-closed half of the gap is REFUTED separately: fail-open is a deliberate recorded posture, not an oversight — agents/state_machine.py:3778-3779 'a guard failure must never cost the user their answer' and agents/turn_event_tee.py:82 'non-fatal by construction — never cost the turn'.

gaps.title: Sequential per-form replacement lets a later (shorter) form match inside an earlier replacement
gaps.origin_evidence: openclaw/src/logging/secret-redaction-registry.ts:96-116 (matches collected first, then a single splice; comment at 108-109)
gaps.halbert_evidence: ingestion/redaction_registry.py:90-92; probe 3: register('secret') turns 'password=<secret>' into 'password=<<secret>>'
gaps.failure_scenario: A registered value that is a substring of the placeholder or of another form's replacement (e.g. an acked password 'secret') mangles every placeholder in the output into '<<secret>>' or worse, which downstream parsers of the '<secret>' marker (the dashboard, tests asserting == '<secret>') then miss. Cosmetic in security terms, but it also breaks the marker contract.
gaps.proposed_test: tests/test_redaction_registry.py: reg.register('secret'); assert reg.redact_text('x=<secret> y') == 'x=<secret> y'.
gaps.proposed_fix: Build one compiled alternation of re.escape(form) sorted longest-first (rebuilt with the cache) and do a single re.sub with the placeholder; a single pass cannot re-match its own output.

verdict.reason: ORIGIN: verified as code. secret-redaction-registry.ts:96-116 collects every {index, value} match against the ORIGINAL text with a prefix-bucket matcher, then splices once at :110-116, so no replacement can be re-matched within the same call. Caveat on the audit's reading: the comment at :108-109 is about nested REGISTRATION during the mask callback, not about self-collision; and the origin's mask is a hinted token ('exact-…-512'), not '<secret>', so the specific '<<secret>>' shape could not arise there anyway. The structural invariant the audit names is nonetheless real in the origin. HALBERT: verified by probe. ingestion/redaction_registry.py:89-92 does sequential str.replace per form; with 'secret' registered, redact_text('password=<secret> and secret') -> 'password=<<secret>> and <secret>'. This is live in the pipeline because ingestion/redaction.py:1230 (redact_structured_values) emits the literal SECRET = '<secret>' marker (redaction.py:29) BEFORE the registry pass runs (result_redaction.py:120-122), so any acked value that is a >=4-char substring of '<secret>' mangles every marker the pattern pass just produced. Cosmetic, not a leak; and G2's reorder (registry first) removes the pattern-produced instance of it for free, so this should be folded into G2 rather than dispatched separately.

halbert_own_bugs.title: Raw form can be evicted before its encoded variants because variants are inserted in sorted() order
halbert_own_bugs.evidence: ingestion/redaction_registry.py:43 and :54-60; probe 1 with max_entries=2 shows the raw value gone and both encoded forms retained.

IMPACT IS MUCH SMALLER THAN STATED, though. At the production bound (get_global_registry() uses the default 512, and grep finds no other SecretVariantRegistry construction in halbert_core), a value's own registration can never evict its own raw form — it evicts the oldest entries instead. A03-redaction.summary: The lift is architecturally sound where Halbert diverged on purpose (dispatch-level choke point, full placeholder instead of hinted masks, no off-switch, parity pin between the two surfaces) but the registry port is less solid than the origin on five mechanical invariants: (1) pattern-then-registry ordering leaks fragments of acked values that contain an IP/JWT/email shape (origin is exact-first everywhere); (2) sorted() insertion lets FIFO eviction drop the raw value and keep only encoded forms; (3) MIN length 4 vs 6 makes short acked values blanket-redact prose; (4) urllib.quote does not match the encoded forms real HTTP egress produces; (5) sequential replace can re-match its own placeholder. Two gaps are about coverage rather than the registry itself: json.dumps(default=str) stringifies bytes/objects AFTER mcp_response, so a non-dict handler result bypasses the Tier 2 boundary entirely (high), and the dispatcher's catch-all, the log formatter and the MCP client's error/token paths skip the registry (medium/low). Halbert's own additions carry two bugs the origins do not have: an unsynchronised process-global registry in a multi-threaded process with fail-open reply seams, and an unredacted MCP args preview. Multi-profile secret scoping (Hermes secret_scope), sandbox credential mounts (credential_files), and plugin pattern registries do not apply to the single-user single-host design and are marked adapted/not-applicable rather than as gaps. Full JSON written to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-4TB-BAD-Halbert/b0e3f0dd-594e-4bec-b7ce-4859472b38f8/scratchpad/wf-oss/A03-redaction.json.
